Older term for the stretch of middle adulthood marked by declining biologic function; in women it is the menopausal period, while in men it has no clear boundary.
An intense reappraisal of one's whole life in middle age, prompted by awareness that life is finite; mostly mental turmoil, with thoughtful rather than impulsive change.
A major, revolutionary turning point in middle age with internal agitation and a flurry of impulsive actions, such as abrupt changes in work or marriage.
A depression some parents develop as the youngest child is about to leave home; most parents feel the departure as a relief.
Erikson's stage of middle adulthood: guiding the next generation or improving society, through children or through helping others, creativity and work.
Bohannan's separation of letting go of the spouse as a love object, a grief reaction for the relationship that takes about 2 years to resolve.
A custody arrangement in which each divorced parent has the child for equal time.
A custody arrangement in which siblings are divided, each parent keeping one or more of the children.
The aging process, a gradual decline in all body systems; from the Latin senescere, to grow old.
Gerontologists' term for people aged 65 to 74.
Gerontologists' term for people aged 75 and older.
Robert Butler's term for discrimination against older people and negative stereotypes of old age.
Erikson's final stage: looking back on life with acceptance, peace and wisdom, or with bitterness that it was too short and cannot be lived again.
Help with daily activities such as bathing, dressing or eating when no skilled medical care is needed; Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care.
